spans.text: This is the third book in a series called The American Firsts, and I have said elsewhere that I do not like the name. With this one the objection changes shape, so I want to put the new version of it here.

The other two events in this series were first at something and were then surpassed, which is its own kind of horror and is the one we are used to. This one has not been surpassed. On the eighteenth of May, 1927, a man blew up a school in Clinton County, Michigan, and killed thirty-eight children, and in the hundred years since, nobody has killed more children in an American school. It is still the record. It has been the record for a century, and the century has included a great deal.
That is a very difficult fact to put on a jacket, and I would rather put it here, where I can say the next part in the same breath.
This book does not go inside the school.

I want that on the first page you read, because it is the single most important thing to know before you decide whether to spend a fortnight with it, and because I would rather lose you now than at page ninety.

There is no corridor in this book, no classroom, no child, no quarter to nine, no superintendent, no truck in the road. The word school appears in these pages almost only as a place her husband goes. If you have come for the disaster you have come to the wrong book, and there are good ones, and I have listed what I used at the back.
What it is about instead
His wife.

Her name was Nellie Kehoe. She was fifty-one, she had asthma, she had been in and out of hospitals in Lansing for eight months, and she was killed at their farm at some point in the thirty-six hours before the school came down. Her body was found on the nineteenth, behind a burned building, laid on a hog chute. The coroner's jury could not say when she died and did not try very hard to find out.

Fifty-five witnesses were sworn over three days at that inquest. Three of them were women who had known her for years. None of the three was called for that reason. The one time in three days that the prosecuting attorney asked any man in that room what Nellie Kehoe had said, he asked it about a New Year's Eve sixteen months earlier, and the answer was that the witness did not know, and nobody followed it up.
On the list of the dead attached to the jury's finding, between Johns and McFarren, there is an entry that reads Kehoe, Mrs. Andrew.
Hers is the only name on that list that is not a name.

That is the book. A woman who has been a subordinate clause in every account of this for a hundred years, given four hundred pages and the first person, in her own kitchen, on her own farm, which was her family's farm before it was his.
The bargain
You know what happens. You knew before you opened this, and the back cover told you anyway.
She does not.

Almost the whole of this book takes place before the eighteenth of May, in a farmhouse, at a kitchen table, and the woman telling it does not know what is coming and is not permitted by me to suspect it. She notices everything. She notices ten boxes of explosive standing in her barn for one soft stump. She notices that the interest has not been paid in five years. She notices two porcelain knobs on the end of a barn on a farm with no electricity, and eight trees girdled at the same height, and a sound under her floor on a January afternoon.

And she concludes almost nothing, because there is almost nothing to conclude, and because the alternative to concluding nothing is to say a sentence out loud about her husband that no woman in that township could have said and been believed.

That gap is the engine and it is the only one this book has. Every chapter is read twice at once: once as what it is, which is a Tuesday on a farm, and once as what you know it to be. She gets the Tuesday.

I have tried very hard not to make any of it ominous. Nothing in this book is arranged so as to be poignant later. When a man mends a neighbour's pump for nothing, he is mending a pump for nothing, and he did that, constantly, for years, and every soul in Clinton County would have told you so and would have been telling the truth.
What I owe you
Four things, and I would rather you had them now than found them at the back.

Nellie Kehoe left seven words. In the winter before she died she had a coughing fit in front of a friend, who said she would go out if she was hurting her, and Nellie said I will hurt you, and the friend said there was nothing in the world she would not do for her, and Nellie said I know it. That is the entire surviving record of this woman speaking. Everything else she says or thinks in this book is mine.

She is alive on the morning of the eighteenth because I decided she was. The jury's window is thirty-six hours wide and the record does not narrow it. I have taken the last hour it allows. A genealogical compilation gives the day before. It may be right, and if it is, the last three chapters of this novel did not happen.

Two people in this book are invented outright: a nurse at the hospital in Lansing, and a neighbouring couple the record mentions and does not identify. Everyone else with a name has it because a document gave it.

The two documents this book is built from were recovered from a dead website. The inquest transcript and the contemporary account written by Kehoe's own neighbour both survive, as far as I can find, only as one man's transcriptions on a personal site whose domain expired in 2018. I got them out of the Internet Archive. Neither is citable and I have verified neither against an original. That is a real hole and it is described properly at the back.

There is a fuller accounting in the Author's Note, and an appendix after it setting out what the record actually contains for Nellie Kehoe, line by line, with the strength of each item marked. If you are the sort of reader who checks, and I hope you are, start there and come back.
One last thing, and it is the fact I did not know when I started and that reorganised the whole book.
The farm was hers.

Not legally. The deed says Andrew P. Kehoe and nothing else. But it was the old Lawrence Price place, and Lawrence Price was her uncle, and they bought it from his executors because it was her family's ground, with six thousand dollars down and six thousand on a mortgage running back to that same estate.
He defaulted on it. For five years. To her dead uncle.

And in March of 1926 the estate's lawyer took five hundred dollars of her own legacy from that uncle and applied it to her husband's unpaid note, and wrote to tell her so, and she wrote back and said that she was glad.
J. L. C.

The coroner of Clinton County is a man named C. E. Lamb and on the nineteenth of May he stands where he is required to stand, which is beside the body, and looks at it for as long as the law asks him to look.
The law does not say how long. The law says view. So he views.

What is left of Emery E. Huyck is under canvas on a plank table in a building that was a store and is now whatever anyone needs it to be. The village has been improvising for a day. There are men in the doorway with their hats in their hands and none of them come in. Lamb lifts the canvas at the head end and lowers it again and writes something short in a notebook, and the writing takes longer than the looking did.
Then he impanels six men.
Edward Drumheller. Ishmell Everett. Burt Wilcox. Wilmer Coleman. Clarence Tolman. Alton Church.

They are farmers, all of them, from townships near enough to have heard it and far enough to have their own children. Each is sworn to inquire on behalf of the people of this State, when, in what manner, and by what means the said Emery E. Huyck came to his death. That is the whole of the question they are given. It is one man, one death, one morning. Everything else that happened in Bath Township on the eighteenth of May is legally a circumstance surrounding it.
Lamb adjourns them to the twenty-third.
On the twenty-third they come back to Bath at half past ten in the morning and the village smells like the fifth day.

It is not smoke exactly. The fires are long out and it has rained once since, and the rain took the ash down into the ground and made the ground smell like a stove. Under that there is wet plaster, and under the plaster there is the sweetish thing that gets into board lumber when board lumber has been rained on and stood in the sun, and under all of it there is the smell of too many automobiles in a place that has never had this many automobiles, gasoline and hot oil and dust ground fine by tires. The Lansing papers have been out here since Wednesday noon. The Detroit papers came Thursday. There is a man from Chicago in a good hat.
The north wing of the school is not there. What is there is a shape, and men have been going into the shape since Wednesday and coming out of it, and there is a rope now.

The room they use is not large. It has a stove that nobody lights and windows on one side that face the road, so that all day the light comes in from the same direction and the men who sit with their backs to the windows are hard to see clearly and the men who face them are lit up like a photograph. There are chairs enough. There are not chairs enough for everyone who wants one, and by the second morning the standing room at the back is three deep and the door is left open, which does nothing for the smell.

The Prosecuting Attorney of Clinton County will conduct the inquiry. His name is William C. Searl. He has a way of asking a question and then waiting past the point where the witness has stopped talking, and the witness fills the wait, and about a third of what is useful in three days comes out of that habit.
Glenn Whitman sits at the end of the table with a machine and takes it down.

Whitman takes down what is said. When a document is handed up and read aloud into the record, Whitman writes the word Reading, in parentheses, and takes down nothing at all. This happens four times in three days.

The witnesses come in the order Searl wants them, which is not the order of the day and not the order of the road. A school board member first, then a janitor, then a boy who was outside, then a man who hauled something, then a neighbour, then another neighbour. Fifty-five people in three days. Some of them are on the stand for forty minutes. Some of them are on for four.
At the end of it there will be a finding, and attached to the finding, forming a part of it, there will be a list.

The list is set in two columns, alphabetical down one and then down the other, family names first. There are no ages on it. There are no schools on it, no grades, no rooms. It is a plain list of names of the sort a clerk makes when a clerk is told to make a list, and it runs Bauerle, Bergen, Bromund, Burnett, Chapman, Clayton, Cochran, Cushman, and on.
In the left column, between Johns, Doris and McFarren, Clarence, there is an entry that reads:
Kehoe, Mrs. Andrew.
In the right column, at the same height on the page, near enough that a man reading down both would take them in together, there is an entry that reads:
Kehoe, Andrew.
Hers is the only name on the list of the dead that is not a name.

Nobody in the room says it aloud on the twenty-third. Searl does not open with it. Lamb does not instruct the jury about it. Of the fifty-five people who will be sworn in this room over the next three days, three are women who knew her, and none of the three is called for that reason, and none of the three is asked the question that would matter.
The proceeding is not required to find out anything about her at all. It is required to find out how one man came to his death in a road at ten minutes past nine in the morning.
Searl calls Albert Detloff.
I went out to look at the west eighty on a Tuesday in November because I wanted to see the stumps.

That is a plain sentence and it is also the first lie I told, and I told it to myself, walking, in my own field, with nobody within half a mile to hear it. I did not want to see the stumps. I wanted to see whether there were any.

It had frozen in the night and thawed by nine and the ground had that give in it that takes the heel of your shoe and keeps a little of it. Corn stubble on the near side, cut and shocked and the shocks gone in already, so it was just the stubble and the crows working it. Past that the line fence, and past the line fence the west eighty, which is grass and second growth and always has been.
I am going to be exact about this because being exact is the only thing I have ever been good at that nobody had to teach me.

Lawrence Price bought four eighties in this township before I was born and they corner on each other like the corners of four handkerchiefs laid down on a table. The one with the house on it is the home eighty. That is what everyone called it and what the papers call it and what I call it. West of the house across the lane is the second, and the west eighty is the far one, and it has never been cleared to plow in my lifetime and it was not cleared in his. It has hickory and some soft maple and a good deal of thorn, and along the low place it has willow, and it was where my uncle put steers when he had steers, and where a boy from the Rounds place used to shoot rabbits with an old single barrel, and where in 1889 or 1890 I was allowed to go with my mother to pick elderberries, which is the first time I remember the smell of that ground.
There were no stumps.

There have not been stumps on the west eighty since before Lawrence Price died and there were not many then. You do not stump ground you are not going to plow. A stump is a thing you fight because it is standing in the middle of something you want, and there was nothing out there anybody wanted but shade and rabbits.

I walked the fence line north to the corner and then east along the top of it and I looked at the ground the whole way like a woman looking for a dropped needle. Thorn. Old grass gone the colour of a paper bag. Two soft maples the size of my wrist, alive. One stump about the width of a dinner plate, rotted down soft enough that I put my shoe on it and it took the shoe, from an elm that came over in a wind before the war.

One. In eighty acres. And it was going back into the ground on its own, which is what they do if you leave them, and it would have taken a man with a mattock about forty minutes to finish what the weather had nearly done.
I stood there in the wind with my hand on a fence post and did the thing I do, which is arithmetic.

Five hundred pounds of explosive is what is standing on the main floor of my barn. Ten boxes. Fifty pounds to a box. I know that because I counted them in October when they came, and I counted them again in November, and I got ten both times, which will tell you something about me.
I should say what I mean by counting, because I do not want anybody supposing it is a nervous habit. It is not. It is a trade.

When my mother died I was eighteen and there were six of them behind me and a father who went out at six and came in at seven, and the way you keep six children alive on one wage is that you know at all times what you have. Not roughly. Exactly. Eleven eggs, not a dozen. Two and a quarter pounds of side pork. A tin with four dollars and sixty cents in it and a note in pencil on the lid saying what the four dollars and sixty cents is already spoken for. I did that from eighteen until I was thirty-seven and by the end of it I could stand in a doorway and tell you the contents of a room the way a man tells you the time by the sun.

It does not go away. I have not needed it since 1912 and it has not gone away. I know how many quart jars are in that cellar and how many of them are peaches. I know that there are nine yards and a bit of the grey wool left because I bought twelve and cut a skirt out of it. I know what the eggs brought in Bath in the second week of October and I know what they brought in the second week of October a year ago, and I know that the difference is four cents, and nobody has ever asked me and I have never once volunteered it.
So when I say five hundred pounds, understand that I am not estimating.
Five hundred pounds for one soft stump the width of a dinner plate.

I want to be understood here. I did not stand at that fence post and think anything. That is not what happened and I will not put it in afterward the way people do. What happened is that I noticed a number was wrong, the way you notice the churn is a quart short, and then I put my hand back in my coat pocket and turned around and started for the house, because the wind was coming out of the northwest and I was already short of breath from the walk out.
The breath is the other thing. I will get to it.

The boxes came home in October in a truck that was not ours, driven by a young fellow from up the road. I was in the kitchen. I heard the truck come in and go around back the way a truck does when it is going to be unloaded, and I looked out and Andrew was walking backward ahead of it with his hand up, guiding him in.

They put them on the main floor of the main barn. Not the mow. Not the granary, not the shed. The main floor, where you drive a wagon straight through, which is the most convenient place on the whole farm to put a thing you intend to move again.

I went out to see, because I always go out to see. He had the tailgate down and the young fellow was handing the boxes and Andrew was taking them and setting them, and he set them in two rows of five with the printing all facing the same way, which is how he does everything, and when they were down he took the barn broom and swept out the truck bed.
I said, that is a good deal of something.
He said, it is pyrotol. The government is selling it off. It came out of the war.
I said, what does it cost.
He said, next to nothing, which is why to buy it now.

That is the whole conversation. I have been over it since the way you go over a room after you have lost an earring in it, and there is nothing in it. He answered me. He answered me pleasantly and correctly and completely, and he did not say what it was for, and I did not ask, and the reason I did not ask is not that I was afraid of him. I would like that understood too.

The young fellow with the truck was Job Sleight's boy. He had his cap on the back of his head and he was pleased with himself for having driven that far and back inside a day. He drank a glass of milk in my kitchen standing up, which is what men do when they believe sitting down would be an imposition, and he said the Jackson road was good most of the way and terrible for about four miles.
I did not ask him anything either.

I am fifty years old. In August I will be fifty-one. I was born Ellen Agnes Price at Zilwaukee in Saginaw County in 1875, and everybody from my mother forward has called me Nellie, and the only people who ever wrote Ellen down were priests and clerks.
I have been Mrs. Andrew Kehoe since 1912, which is thirteen years, and I have lived in this house since 1919, which is six.

But I have known this house since I was a girl, and that is the part that matters and the part nobody in this township quite has hold of, because they all came later or they were children when I was already grown.

Lawrence Price built it. He was my father's brother. He built it the way a man builds when he has decided he is going to be somebody in a township, which is to say a little larger than he needed and square, front door in the middle, two windows either side, a porch straight across. Inside, a hall running through and the stairs on the left going up. Ash floors. Plaster over lath. A parlour on the right that no one sat in on a weekday in thirty years, a dining room behind it, the kitchen across the back with the pantry off it, and a cellar under the whole of it with a stone wall and a dirt floor and an outside cellarway with two slanted doors.
I could walk it in the dark. I have.

There is a crack in the sill of the north window in the dining room that has been there since 1891 and it is shaped like the state of Michigan if you are a child and you want it to be. There is a place at the bottom of the stairs where the third baluster is loose and turns in your hand and has always turned, and my uncle said every year that he would get to it. The pantry has four shelves and the second one down is deeper than the others by about two inches, because the man who did the carpentry ran short of a board and let it out.

When I came here a bride of thirty-seven, a woman with grey already at her temples, married for the first time in front of a priest who had baptised her, I went into that pantry and put my hand flat on the deep shelf and did not say a word about it to anybody.

Ann Rounds across the road has known me since I was about fourteen. Before that, even. She says it in exactly that way and it is true. When I came back here married she came over with a cake and she did not say welcome. She said, well, you are home. I have been grateful for that sentence for thirteen years and I have never told her so.

My people were not in this township. My father took us to Lansing, and there was a stretch at Saginaw before that, and my mother died in 1893 when I was eighteen, and after that where my people were was wherever I was, which was a kitchen with six children behind me and the youngest of them three years old. But my uncle was here and the farm was here, and I was sent out summers, and the ground I learned as a child is this ground.
We bought it in 1919 from his executors. Twelve thousand dollars. Six down out of the sale of the Tecumseh place and six on a mortgage back to the estate.

I am not going to talk about the money yet. Not because it is a secret. Because it is January's business and this is November, and I am telling it in the order it came to me, and in November of 1925 the money was a thing I had the shape of in my mind the way you know without looking that there is a chair behind you.
What I had in November of 1925 was a walk out to the west eighty, and a wind, and no stumps.

I came back in along the lane. The lane runs from the road past the house, and the buildings stand north of it in a row: the main barn first, then the little barn, then the hog house, then the corn crib, and the chicken house off by itself. My uncle set them with room between and it is a well-laid-out farm. Everybody says so. The man who said so most often was Andrew, and he said it to me like a compliment, as though I had laid it out myself, as though the whole place were a thing I had brought with me into the marriage.
The main barn doors were shut. I stopped in the lane and did not open them.

I want that down, whatever this is. I stopped in the lane in my coat, out of breath, with my own barn eight feet off me and the doors on a hasp with no lock in it, and I did not open them and count the boxes a third time. The reason is that I had counted them twice and the number was not going to have changed, and a woman who goes and counts a thing a third time is a woman who is looking for something other than the number.
I went in and washed my hands and put the kettle over.

He came in at half past five with the lantern and hung it and washed and sat down and ate what I gave him, which was pork and boiled potatoes and the last of the cabbage and a pie I had made Monday, because Monday I had wind enough to make a pie. He eats neatly and without hurry and without a word until he is nearly through, and then he told me that Monty Ellsworth's boiler at the slaughterhouse had a seam going, and that Monty had asked him about it, and that he would go down in the morning and look at it.
I said, is he paying you.
He said, no.
I said, he ought to.
He said, I would not take it.

And then he smiled at me, and it was a real smile and it reached his eyes, and he said, they know where to come, Nell. Then he got up and carried his own plate to the sink, which he has done every day of thirteen years, and which not one man in this township does.
Here is what I did that night.

I got the supper things done and trimmed the lamp and sat in the dining room with the mending basket and did the heel of a sock and half of a torn sheet, and when he had gone up I sat on a while by myself.
What I thought about was not the barn.

What I thought about was that in the spring, if there was money, I would like the north sash out and the sill mended, and that the crack in it had been there thirty-four years, and that I had been looking at it since I was a girl in a pinafore and it had not got any worse. A house will go on a very long time with something wrong with it, if the thing that is wrong is small and stays where you put it.
Then I went up.
There is one more piece of that November and I will set it down because it belongs with the rest, and because it is the only part of it any other living person could tell you.

Some time that month, going in to Bath with eggs, I met Ann Rounds at the corner, and we stood in the road and talked about nothing, and she asked after my chest, because she asks, and I said it was middling, and she said the cold always tells on you, Nellie, and I said it does.
Then she said, Andy was over Saturday and put a new pin in our whiffletree and would not hear of a thing for it.
And I said, that sounds like him.
And she said, we are lucky in our neighbours.
And I said, yes.
I said yes.

I have gone over that too and I do not find that I lied. He was over Saturday. He did put in the pin. He would not hear of a thing for it. He was going to fix Monty Ellsworth's boiler and it was not going to cost Monty a cent, and there is not a soul from here to Gunnisonville who would not tell you the same about Andrew Kehoe, and every one of them would be telling the truth.
I would like that understood before any of the rest of it. Everybody here was telling the truth.

In the morning it rained, and by noon it had turned to a wet snow that did not lie, and he went down to Ellsworth's about the boiler, and I made bread, and the ten boxes stood on the main floor of the main barn where a wagon goes through, in two rows of five, with the printing all facing the same way.
